elements.id-string-4: \normalsizeMolecular conformer generation (MCG) is an important task in cheminformatics and drug discovery.The ability to efficiently generate low-energy 3D structures can avoid expensive quantum mechanical simulations, leading to accelerated screenings and enhanced structural exploration.Several generative models have been developed for MCG, but many struggle to consistently produce high-quality conformers.To address these issues, we introduce \modelns, which coarse-grains molecular graphs based on torsional angles and integrates them into an SE(3)-equivariant hierarchical variational autoencoder.Through equivariant coarse-graining, we aggregate the fine-grained atomic coordinates of subgraphs connected via rotatable bonds, creating a variable-length coarse-grained latent representation.Our model uses a novel aggregated attention mechanism to restore fine-grained coordinates from the coarse-grained latent representation, enabling efficient autoregressive generation of large molecules.Furthermore, our work expands current conformer generation benchmarks and introduces new metrics to better evaluate the quality and viability of generated conformers.We demonstrate that \model generates more accurate conformer ensembles compared to prior generative models and traditional cheminformatics methods.\footnote{Code will be available at \url{https://github.com/ASK-Berkeley/CoarsenConf}.}
elements.id-string-7: Molecular conformer generation (MCG) is a fundamental task in computational chemistry.
elements.id-string-8: The objective is to predict stable low-energy 3D molecular structures, known as conformers.
elements.id-string-9: Accurate molecular conformations are crucial for a wide range of applications that depend on precise spatial and geometric qualities, including drug discovery and protein docking.
elements.id-string-10: In traditional physics-based methods, there is a trade-off between speed and accuracy.
elements.id-string-11: Quantum mechanical methods, such as CREST \citep{CREST}, are accurate but computationally slow, while stochastic cheminformatics-based methods like RDKit EKTDG~\citep{rdkit} provide more efficient but less accurate results.
elements.id-string-12: As the difficulty of computing low-energy structures increases with the number of atoms and rotatable bonds in a molecule, there has been interest in developing machine learning (ML) methods to generate efficient and accurate conformer predictions.

elements.id-string-14: Prior generative models have shown success in the current benchmarks used to evaluate the accuracy of conformer predictions~\citep{mit_background}.
elements.id-string-15: However, current benchmarks~\citep{CVGAE} are problematic as for a molecule with $L$ known conformers, they measure the minimum error of the best conformer out of a model-generated set of size $2L$.
elements.id-string-16: We contend that this is an inherently flawed metric, as by failing to penalize a success rate or validity of $\frac{1}{2L}$, prior benchmarks do not accomplish their goal of assessing a model's accuracy and ability to generalize.
elements.id-string-17: Poor model performance is essentially masked out as long as one good conformer exists.
elements.id-string-19: Only measuring the best error to a single conformer is not comprehensive, as not all conformers are likely to appear in the real world.
elements.id-string-20: Additionally, despite knowing the error associated with the optimal conformer, even determining the optimal conformer among the available $2L$ options without prior knowledge of the ideal structure remains a considerable challenge.
elements.id-string-21: Thus, these metrics are not fully informative as to whether current models will be useful for downstream tasks such as protein docking, which depends on highly accurate 3D structures.
elements.id-string-22: In this work, we further discuss the implications of these flaws and provide new comprehensive metrics as a step towards better-measuring model performance.
elements.id-string-23: We also show that by applying a built-in relatively inexpensive force field optimization, RDKit, an open-source cheminformatics software, predominantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods, especially on our new metrics.
elements.id-string-24: Our improved metrics also serve as motivation for improving conformer generative modeling at an architectural level.
elements.id-string-25: To this end, we introduce \modelns, an SE(3)-equivariant hierarchical VAE that pools information from fine-grain atomic coordinates to a coarse-grain subgraph level representation for efficient autoregressive conformer generation.
elements.id-string-26: Coarse-graining reduces the dimensionality of the problem allowing conditional autoregressive generation rather than generating all coordinates independently, as done in prior work.
elements.id-string-27: By directly conditioning on the 3D coordinates of prior generated subgraphs, our model better generalizes across chemically and spatially similar subgraphs.
elements.id-string-28: This mimics the underlying molecular synthesis process, in which small functional units bond together to form large drug-like molecules.
elements.id-string-29: Unlike prior methods, \model generates low-energy conformers with the ability to model atomic coordinates, distances, and torsion angles directly.
elements.id-string-30: Our main contributions are as follows:
elements.id-string-32: We present \modelns, a novel conditional hierarchical VAE.
elements.id-string-33: \model learns a coarse-grained subgraph-level latent distribution for efficient SE(3)-equivariant autoregressive conformer generation.Our coarse-graining strategy allows \model to learn optimal torsional angles implicitly.To our knowledge, this is the first method to use coarse-graining in the context of MCG and the first to explore 3D autoregressive techniques for MCG.\model is the first model capable of handling variable-length coarse-to-fine generation using an aggregated attention strategy.
elements.id-string-34: Prior coarse-to-fine methods~\citep{CGVAE} require the number of coarse-grain beads to be fixed for all input molecules and focused on the task of coarse-to-fine backmapping.We predominantly outperform prior methods on GEOM-QM9 and GEOM-DRUGS evaluation benchmarks \citep{GEOM}.
elements.id-string-35: We do so while requiring less training time, 2\% the total training iterations, and 59\% and 92.7\% less data compared to prior state-of-the-art for QM9 and DRUGS, respectively.We enhance the existing benchmarks for conformer generation by incorporating direct measurements of average and maximum root mean square deviation (RMSD) across the set of generated conformers for each molecule.

elements.id-string-38: \paragraph{Notations.} We represent each molecule as a graph $\gG =  (\gV, \gE)$, where $\gV$ is the set of vertices representing atoms and $\gE$ is the set of edges representing inter-atomic bonds.
elements.id-string-39: Each node $v$ in $\gV$ describes the chosen atomic features such as element type, atomic charge, and hybridization state.
elements.id-string-40: Each edge $e_{uv}$ in $\gE$ describes the corresponding chemical bond connecting $u$ and $v$, and is labeled with its bond type.
elements.id-string-41: Following \citet{GraphDG}, each molecular graph is expanded to incorporate auxiliary edges connecting all atoms within a 4\AA\ radius to enhance long-range interactions in message passing.
elements.id-string-42: The spatial position of each atom in $\gV$ is represented by a 3D coordinate vector $\vr \in \sR^{3}$, such that the full molecule conformation is represented by the matrix $\mX \in \sR^{|\gV| \times 3}$.
elements.id-string-43: \paragraph{Problem Definition.} \emph{Molecular conformation generation} (MCG) is a conditional generative process that aims to model the conditional distribution of 3D molecular conformations $\mX$, given the 2D molecule graph $\gG$, \ie, $p(\mX | \gG)$.
elements.id-string-44: While prior works have shown some success with learning 3D conformations starting with only the 2D information, many require complex and compute-intensive architectures \citep{DMCG, unimol}.
elements.id-string-45: Recently, \citet{torsional-diffusion} demonstrated good performance on the GEOM-DRUGS dataset by priming the method with easy-to-obtain 3D approximations via RDKit EKTDG \citep{rdkit}.
elements.id-string-46: \citet{torsional-diffusion} showed that RDKit is highly effective at generating conformations with correct inter-atomic distances and, as a result, can constrain the problem to a diffusion process only over torsion angles.
elements.id-string-47: We thus formalize MCG as modeling the conditional distribution $p(\mX | \gR)$, where $\gR$ = $\langle \gV, \gE, \gX \rangle$ and $\gX$ is the RDKit generated atomic coordinates.
elements.id-string-48: This is functionally the same underlying distribution as $p(\mX | \gG)$, as we use RDKit as a building block to provide an approximation starting from only 2D information.
elements.id-string-49: We will show that more robust conformers are generated by conditioning on approximations without imposing explicit angular and distance constraints.
elements.id-string-50: \paragraph{Classical Methods for Conformer Generation.} A molecular conformer refers to the collection of 3D structures that are energetically favorable and correspond to local minima of the potential energy surface.
elements.id-string-51: CREST~\citep{CREST} uses semi-empirical tight-binding density functional theory for energy calculations, which, while computationally less expensive than ab-initio quantum mechanical (QM) methods, still requires approximately 90 core hours per drug-like molecule~\citep{GEOM}.
elements.id-string-52: Though CREST was used to generate the ground truth GEOM dataset, it is too slow for downstream applications such as high-throughput virtual screening.
elements.id-string-53: Cheminformatics methods, such as RDKit EKTDG, are commonly used to quickly generate approximate low-energy conformations of molecules.
elements.id-string-54: These methods are less accurate than QM methods due to the sparse coverage of the conformational space resulting from stochastic sampling.
elements.id-string-55: Additionally, force field optimizations are inherently less accurate than the above QM methods.
elements.id-string-56: RDKit EKTDG employs a genetic algorithm for Distance Geometry optimization that can be enhanced with a molecular mechanics force field optimization (MMFF).
elements.id-string-57: \citet{rdkit-cluster} recently highlighted potential flaws in the current MCG benchmarks and demonstrated how EKTDG, in conjunction with a traditional sampling and clustering procedure, can outperform many recent deep learning methods.
elements.id-string-58: To overcome the accuracy-efficiency trade-off in classical methods, we combine easy-to-obtain classical approximations with efficient data-driven strategies to improve the generalization of robust MCG.
elements.id-string-59: \paragraph{Deep Learning Methods for Conformer Generation.} Several probabilistic deep learning methods for MCG have been developed~\citep{generative_background}, such as variational autoencoders in CVGAE \citep{CVGAE} and ConfVAE \citep{ConfVAE}, normalizing flows in CGCF \citep{CGCF}, score-based generative models in ConfGF \citep{ConfGF} and DGSM \citep{DGSM}, and diffusion models in GeoDiff \citep{geodiff} and Torsional Diffusion \citep{torsional-diffusion}.
elements.id-string-60: GraphDG \citep{GraphDG} forgoes modeling coordinates and angles, relying solely on distance geometry.
elements.id-string-61: DMCG \citep{DMCG} and Uni-Mol \citep{unimol} present examples of effective large models, the first mimicking the architecture of AlphaFold \citep{alphafold} and the second using large-scale SE(3)-equivariant transformer pretraining.
elements.id-string-62: \paragraph{Molecular Coarse-graining.} Molecular coarse-graining refers to the simplification of a molecule representation by grouping the fine-grained (FG) atoms in the original structure into individual coarse-grained (CG) beads $\gB$ with a rule-based mapping.
elements.id-string-63: Coarse-graining has been widely utilized in protein design \citep{CGProt-background, CGProtein} and molecular dynamics~\citep{cg-force-field}, and analogously fragment-level or subgraph-level generation has proven to be highly valuable in diverse 2D molecule design tasks \citep{FaST}.
elements.id-string-64: Breaking down generative problems into smaller pieces is an approach that can be applied to several 3D molecule tasks.
elements.id-string-65: For instance, CGVAE \citep{CGVAE} learns a latent distribution to back map or restore FG coordinates from a fixed number of CG beads effectively.
elements.id-string-66: We note that various different coarse-graining strategies exist~\citep{cg-survey, arts2023diffusion, CG-MD, cg_thermo}, and many require the ability to represent inputs with a non-fixed granularity.
elements.id-string-67: To handle this, \model uses a flexible variable-length CG representation that is compatible with all coarse-graining techniques.
elements.id-string-68: \paragraph{Autoregressive Molecule Generation.} Autoregressive models provide control over the generative process by enabling direct conditioning on prior information, allowing for a more precise and targeted generation of output.
elements.id-string-69: Autoregressive generation has shown success in 2D molecule tasks using SMILE-based methods, as seen in MolMIM~\citep{reidenbach2023improving}, as well as graph-based atom-wise and subgraph-level techniques, as shown in GraphAF \citep{graphaf} and HierVAE \citep{HierVAE}.
elements.id-string-70: Similarly, 3DLinker \citep{3dlinker} and SQUID \citep{squid} showcase the usefulness of 3D autoregressive molecule generation and their ability to leverage conditional information in both atom-wise and subgraph-level settings for 3D linkage and shape-conditioned generative tasks respectively.
elements.id-string-71: We note that, unlike prior methods~\citep{squid}, \model does not require a predefined fragment vocabulary.
elements.id-string-72: HERN~\citep{jin2022antibody} further demonstrates the power of hierarchical equivariant autoregressive methods in the task of computational 3D antibody design.
elements.id-string-73: \paragraph{SE(3)-Equivariance.} Let $\gX$ and $\gY$ be the input and output vector spaces, respectively, which possess a set of transformations $G$: $G\times\gX\rightarrow\gX$ and $G\times\gY\rightarrow\gY$.
elements.id-string-74: The function $\phi: \gX\rightarrow\gY$ is called equivariant with respect to $G$ if when we apply any transformation to the input, the output also changes via the same transformation or under a certain predictable behavior, \ie,
elements.id-string-76: The function $\phi: \gX\mapsto\gY$ is $G$-equivariant if it commutes with any transformation in $G$,
elements.id-string-79: where $\rho_{\gX}$ and $\rho_{\gY}$ are the group representations in the input and output space, respectively.
elements.id-string-80: Specifically, $\phi$ is called invariant if $\rho_\gY$ is the identity.
elements.id-string-81: By enforcing SE(3)-equivariance in our probabilistic model,  $p(\mX | \gR)$ remains unchanged for any rototranslation of the approximate conformer $\gR$.
elements.id-string-82: \modelns's architecture is inspired by recent equivariant graph neural network architectures, such as EGNN \citep{EGNN} and PaiNN \citep{painn}, as well as Vector Neuron multi-layer perceptron (VN-MLP) \citep{vn-mlp}.

elements.id-string-97: \paragraph{Learning Framework.} \model is a conditional generative model that learns $p(X | \gR)$ where $X$ is the low-energy 3D conformation, and $\gR$ is the RDKit best guess conformation.
elements.id-string-98: Specifically, we optimize $p(X | \gR)$ by maximizing its variational lower bound with an approximate posterior distribution $q_\phi(z |X, \gR)$ and learned prior $p_\psi(z | \gR)$:
elements.id-string-99: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \log p(X|\gR) \geq & \underbrace{\E_{q_\phi(z | X, \gR)} \log p_\theta(X | \gR, z)}_{\gL_{\text{reconstruction}}} + \underbrace{\E_{q_\phi(z | X, \gR)} \log \frac{ p_\psi(z|\gR) }{q_\phi(z| X, \gR)}}_{\gL_{\text{latent regularization}}},  \end{aligned} \end{equation}
elements.id-string-100: where $q_\phi(z|X,\gR)$ is the hierarchical equivariant encoder model, $p_\theta(X|\gR,z)$ is the equivariant decoder model to recover $X$ from $\gR$ and $z$, and $p_\psi(z|\gR)$ is the learned prior distribution.
elements.id-string-101: The reconstruction loss, $\gL_{\text{recon.}}$, is implemented as $\text{MSE}(\gA(X_{true}, X_{model}), X_{model})$, where $\gA$ is the Kabsch alignment function that provides an optimal rotation matrix and translation vector to minimize the mean squared error (MSE) \citep{Kabsch}.
elements.id-string-102: The second term, $\gL_{\text{reg.}}$, can be viewed as a regularization over the latent space and is implemented as $\beta D_{KL}(q_\phi(z | X, \gR)\parallel p_\psi(z|\gR))$ \citep{beta-vae}.
elements.id-string-103: In practice, we add an auxiliary loss function that measures the distance error between the coordinates of all 2-hop neighbors in the molecular graph.
elements.id-string-104: More details on the loss function are in Appendix~\sref{section:appendix-loss-func}.
elements.id-string-105: \paragraph{Learning Optimal Distortions.} As the goal of MCG is to model the conditional distribution $p(X | \gR)$, we can simplify the learning objective by setting $X = \gR + \Delta X$ and learn the optimal distortion $\Delta X$ from the RDKit approximation.
elements.id-string-106: This greatly simplifies the learning objective, as we have ensured $\gL_{\text{recon.}}$ is no worse than that of the RDKit approximation.
elements.id-string-107: This procedure is analogous to using multiple sequence alignments in protein structure prediction tasks to initialize the model in an approximate low-energy state \citep{alphafold}.
elements.id-string-108: We stress that the RDKit approximate conformers are trivial to obtain compared to the cost of generative model training and inference.
elements.id-string-110: \paragraph{Hierarchical Modules.} We describe the encoder, shown in~\fref{fig:schematic}(I).
elements.id-string-111: The model operates over SE(3)-invariant atom features $h \in R^{n\times D}$, and SE(3)-equivariant atomistic coordinates $x \in R^{n\times3}$.
elements.id-string-112: A single encoder layer is composed of three modules: fine-grained, pooling, and coarse-grained.
elements.id-string-113: Full equations for each module can be found in Appendix \sref{section:eqn-fine}, \sref{section:eqn-pool}, \sref{section:eqn-coarse}, respectively.
elements.id-string-114: The fine-grained module is a graph-matching message-passing architecture.
elements.id-string-115: It differs from~\citet{equibind} by not having internal closed-form distance regularization and exclusively using unidirectional attention.
elements.id-string-116: Its purpose is to effectively match the approximate conformer and ground truth by updating attention from the former to the latter.
elements.id-string-117: The pooling module takes in the updated representations ($h$ and $x$) of both the ground truth molecule and the RDKit reference from the FG module.
elements.id-string-118: The pooling module is similar to the FG module, except it no longer uses attention and operates over a pooling graph.
elements.id-string-119: Given a molecule with $n$ atoms and $N$ CG beads, the pooling graph consists of $n + N$ nodes.
elements.id-string-120: There is a single directional edge from all atoms to their respective beads (see~\fref{fig:novelty}(I)).
elements.id-string-121: This allows message passing to propagate information through the predefined coarsening strategy.
elements.id-string-122: The coarse-grained module uses the updated CG representations ($H\in R^{N\times D}$ and $X \in R^{N\times 3}$) from the pooling module to learn equivariant CG features ($Z$ and $\Tilde{Z} \in R^{N\times F \times 3}$) for the ground truth molecule and the RDKit reference.
elements.id-string-123: $F$ is fixed as a hyperparameter for latent space size.
elements.id-string-124: $N$ is allowed to be variable-length to handle molecules resulting from any coarsening procedure.
elements.id-string-125: The CG features are learned using a graph-matching point convolution~\citep{tensor-field-network} with similar unidirectional attention as the FG module.
elements.id-string-126: Prior to the main message-passing operations, the input features undergo equivariant mixing~\citep{3dlinker} to further distill geometric information into the learned CG representation.
elements.id-string-127: The modules in each encoder layer communicate with the respective module of the previous layer.
elements.id-string-128: This hierarchical message-passing scheme results in an informative and geometrically grounded final CG latent representation.
elements.id-string-129: We note that the pooling module of layer $\ell$ uses the updated invariant features $H$ from the CG module of layer $\ell - 1$, as shown by the dashed lines in~\fref{fig:schematic}(I).

elements.id-string-135: We found that setting $\sigma_\psi = 1$ results in smoother optimization rather than requiring an additional latent regularization to the standard normal as seen in \citet{CVGAE}.

elements.id-string-142: \paragraph{Channel Selection.} To explicitly handle all choices of coarse-graining techniques, our model performs variable-length backmapping.
elements.id-string-143: This aspect is crucial because every molecule can be coarsened into a different number of beads, and there is no explicit limit to the number of atoms a single bead can represent.
elements.id-string-144: Unlike CGVAE~\citep{CGVAE}, which requires training a separate model for each choice in granularity $N$, \model is capable of reconstructing FG coordinates from any $N$ (illustrated in \fref{fig:schematic}(III)).
elements.id-string-145: CGVAE defines the process of channel selection as selecting the top $k$ latent channels, where $k$ is the number of atoms in a CG bead of interest.
elements.id-string-146: Instead of discarding all learned information in the remaining $F-k$ channels in the latent representation, we use a novel aggregated attention mechanism.
elements.id-string-147: This mechanism learns the optimal mixing of channels to reconstruct the FG coordinates and is illustrated in~\fref{fig:attention}.
elements.id-string-148: The attention operation allows us to actively query our latent representation for the number of atoms we need, and draw upon similarities to the learned RDKit approximation that has been distilled into the latent space through the encoding process.
elements.id-string-149: Channel selection translates the CG latent tensor $Z \in R^{N\times F \times 3}$ into FG coordinates $X_{CC} \in R^{n\times 3}$.
elements.id-string-150: \paragraph{Autoregressive Refinement.} Once channel selection is complete, we have effectively translated the variable-length CG representation back into the desired FG form.
elements.id-string-151: From here, $X_{CC}$ is grouped into its corresponding CG beads, but left in FG coordinates to do a bead-wise autoregressive generation of final low-energy coordinates (\fref{fig:schematic}(IV)).
elements.id-string-152: As there is no intrinsic ordering of subgraphs, we use a breadth-first search that prioritizes larger subgraphs with large out-degrees.
elements.id-string-153: In other words, we generate a linear order that focuses on the largest, most connected subgraphs and works outward.
elements.id-string-154: We believe that by focusing on the most central component first, which occupies the most 3D volume, we can reduce the propagation of error that is typically observed in autoregressive approaches.
elements.id-string-155: We stress that by coarse-graining by torsion angle connectivity, our model learns the optimal torsion angles in an unsupervised manner as the conditional input to the decoder is not aligned.
elements.id-string-156: \model ensures each next generated subgraph is rotated properly to achieve a low coordinate and distance error.

elements.id-string-197: \paragraph{Metrics.} We report both RMSD (AR) and Coverage for Recall (R) and Precision (P).
elements.id-string-198: Recall measures the number of ground truth conformers that are correctly predicted, and Precision measures the accuracy of the generated conformers.
elements.id-string-199: Following \citet{torsional-diffusion}, we generate two times the number of ground truth conformers for each molecule.
elements.id-string-200: More formally, for $K=2L$ let $\{C^*_l\}_{l \in [1, L]}$ and $\{C_k\}_{k \in [1, K]}$ be respectively the sets of ground truth and generated conformers:
elements.id-string-201: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned}  &\text{COV($f$)-R} := \frac{1}{L}\, \bigg\lvert\{ l \in [1..L]: f_{ k\in [1..K]} \rmsd(C_k, C^*_l) < \delta \} \bigg\rvert, &\text{AR($f$)-R} := \frac{1}{L} \sum_{l \in [1..L]}  f_{ k\in [1..K]} \rmsd(C_k, C^*_l), &\text{$f()$} := \{{\min, \mean, \max}\}, \end{aligned} \end{equation}
elements.id-string-203: The precision metrics are obtained by swapping ground truth and generated conformers.
elements.id-string-204: During a true test-time evaluation, the ground truth conformation is unknown.
elements.id-string-205: Therefore, we cannot compare it to all $2L$ generated structures to determine the most accurate one for the downstream application.
elements.id-string-206: Thus, the additions of average (mean) and worst-case (max) evaluation allow us to measure the robustness of the generative model by providing an error bound on each sample.
elements.id-string-207: As most downstream tasks that use molecular conformers possess expensive oracle functions, \ie\ protein docking, it is important to be able to generate optimal conformers, as testing all $2L$ samples for each molecule may be infeasible.
elements.id-string-208: We note that AR is the central task-agnostic metric.
elements.id-string-209: Coverage is derived from AR and its threshold can be chosen arbitrarily, with its value being task-dependent.

elements.id-string-234: We present \modelns, a novel approach for robust molecular conformer generation that combines an SE(3)-equivariant hierarchical VAE with geometric coarse-graining techniques for autoregressive conformer generation.
elements.id-string-235: By utilizing easy-to-obtain approximate conformations, our model effectively learns the optimal distortion to generate low-energy conformers.

elements.id-string-404: \normalsizeMolecular conformer generation (MCG) is an important task in cheminformatics and drug discovery.The ability to efficiently generate low-energy 3D structures can avoid expensive quantum mechanical simulations, leading to accelerated virtual screenings and enhanced structural exploration.Several generative models have been developed for MCG, but many struggle to consistently produce high-quality conformers.To address these issues, we introduce \modelns, which coarse-grains molecular graphs based on torsional angles and integrates them into an SE(3)-equivariant hierarchical variational autoencoder.Through equivariant coarse-graining, we aggregate the fine-grained atomic coordinates of subgraphs connected via rotatable bonds, creating a variable-length coarse-grained latent representation.Our model uses a novel aggregated attention mechanism to restore fine-grained coordinates from the coarse-grained latent representation, enabling efficient generation of accurate conformers.Furthermore, we evaluate the chemical and biochemical quality of our generated conformers on multiple downstream applications, including property prediction and oracle-based protein docking.Overall, \model generates more accurate conformer ensembles compared to prior generative models.
elements.id-string-405: Accurate molecular conformations are crucial for various applications that depend on precise spatial and geometric qualities, including drug discovery and protein docking.
elements.id-string-406: For MCG, traditional physics-based methods present a trade-off between speed and accuracy.
elements.id-string-407: Quantum mechanical methods are more accurate but computationally slow, while stochastic cheminformatics-based methods like RDKit EKTDG~\citep{rdkit} provide more efficient but less accurate results.
elements.id-string-408: As the difficulty of computing low-energy structures increases with the number of atoms and rotatable bonds in a molecule, there has been interest in developing machine learning (ML) methods to generate accurate conformer predictions efficiently.
elements.id-string-409: Existing generative MCG ML models can be broadly classified based on two primary criteria: (1) the choice of the architecture to model the distribution of low-energy conformers and (2) the manner in which they incorporate geometric information to model 3D conformers.
elements.id-string-410: A majority of these methods utilize a single geometric representation, such as distance matrices, atom coordinates, or torsional angles, and pair them with various probabilistic modeling techniques, including variational autoencoders (VAEs) and diffusion models.
elements.id-string-411: A recurring limitation of these prior approaches is that they are restricted to modeling only one specific aspect of geometric information \ie, coordinates or angles.
elements.id-string-412: By restricting themselves to either a pure coordinate or angle space, they often fail to fully leverage the full geometric information inherent to the problem.
elements.id-string-413: Consequently, in this work, we introduce a more flexible molecular latent representation that seamlessly integrates multiple desired geometric modalities, thereby enhancing the overall accuracy and versatility of conformer generation.
elements.id-string-414: To create this flexible representation, we use a process known as coarse-graining to distill molecular information into a simplified, coarse-grained (CG) representation based on specific coarsening criteria.
elements.id-string-415: This is analogous to previous 2D fragment-based generative techniques~\citep{FaST}.
elements.id-string-416: In these scenarios, the fragmentation of molecules into prominent substructures led to significant enhancements in representation learning and generative tasks.
elements.id-string-417: Coarse-graining has seen success in related ML applications like molecular dynamics and protein modeling~\citep{CG-MD, CGProt-background}.
elements.id-string-418: However, these ML approaches have primarily explored rigid coarsening criteria, such as distance-based nearest neighbor methods, which represent all inputs with a fixed granularity or number of beads (\ie\ CG nodes, $N$).
elements.id-string-419: ML models that use fixed-length coarse-graining often necessitate $N$ be fixed for all input molecules~\citep{CGProtein}.
elements.id-string-420: This approach may not be suitable for all scenarios, especially when navigating multi-modal datasets of drug-like molecules of varying sizes (multiple $N$), which better reflects real-world conditions.
elements.id-string-421: To address the limitations of fixed-length CG representations, we introduce \textit{Aggregated Attention} for variable-length coarse-graining (see~\fref{fig:variable_legnth}).
elements.id-string-422: This methodology allows a single latent representation to accommodate molecules with different numbers of fine-grained (FG) atoms and CG beads.
elements.id-string-423: The inherent flexibility of the attention mechanism allows input molecules to be fragmented along torsion angles, enabling the modeling of interatomic distances, 3D atom coordinates, and torsion angles in an equivariant manner, regardless of the molecule's shape or size.
elements.id-string-424: Through Aggregated Attention, we also harness information from the entire learned representation, unlike preceding approaches that restrict the backmapping (from CG back to FG) to a subset~\citep{CGVAE}.
elements.id-string-425: The adaptability of our learned variable-length representations enables more accurate generation.
elements.id-string-426: \begin{figure}[t]  \includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth]{figures/Variable_Length3.png}   \caption{\textbf{Learning flexible coarse-grained representations.}  \model is the first model to employ variable-length (on left) coarse-graining. Each input molecule ($n$ fine-grained (FG) atoms) can be represented by a different number of coarse-grained (CG) nodes $N$, thus accommodating diverse molecular sizes. In contrast, prior approaches rely on fixed-length (on right)  coarse-graining, thereby forcing all molecules to possess the same number of CG nodes. Variable-length coarse-graining enhances the model's ability to create better learned representations across molecules of different sizes and geometries. The molecules on the left are coarsened along torsional angles.}    \end{figure}
elements.id-string-427: Our full innovations are encapsulated in \modelns, an SE(3)-equivariant hierarchical VAE.
elements.id-string-428: Unlike prior MCG methods, \model generates low-energy conformers with the ability to model atomic coordinates (FG and CG), distances, and torsion angles directly via variable-length coarse-graining.
elements.id-string-429: \model learns a coarse-grained or subgraph-level latent distribution for SE(3)-equivariant conformer generation.To our knowledge, this is the first method to use coarse-graining in the context of MCG.\model is the first model capable of handling variable-length coarse-to-fine generation using an \textit{Aggregated Attention} strategy.\model employs a single flexible variable-length node-level latent representation that can uniquely represent molecules of any size with any number of coarse-grained nodes.Furthermore, variable-length coarse-graining circumvents having to train separate generative models for each number of CG beads to represent the same molecular dataset accurately (100+ models for MCG), which is a limitation of fixed-length methods~\citep{CGProtein}.We predominantly outperform prior methods on GEOM-QM9 and GEOM-DRUGS for RMSD precision and property prediction benchmarks \citep{GEOM}.
elements.id-string-430: We also produce a lower overall RMSD distribution across all conformers, achieving this with an order of magnitude less training time compared to prior methods.We evaluate \model on multiple downstream applications to assess the chemical and biochemical quality of our generated conformers, including oracle-based protein docking~\citep{tdc} (the affinity of generated conformers to bind to specific protein pockets) under both flexible and rigid conformational energy minimizations.
elements.id-string-431: Despite lacking prior knowledge about the protein or the downstream task, \model generates significantly better binding ligand conformers for known protein binding sites when compared to prior MCG methods for both oracle scenarios.
elements.id-string-432: \paragraph{Notations.} We represent each molecule as a graph $\emG =  (\gV, \gE)$, where $\gV$ is the set of vertices representing atoms and $\gE$ is the set of edges representing inter-atomic bonds.
elements.id-string-433: \paragraph{Problem Definition.} \emph{Molecular conformation generation} (MCG) is a conditional generative process that aims to model the conditional distribution of 3D molecular conformations $\mX$, given the 2D molecule graph $\emG$, \ie, $p(\mX | \emG)$.
elements.id-string-434: Recently, \citet{torsional-diffusion} demonstrated good performance on the GEOM-DRUGS dataset by priming the method with easy-to-obtain 3D approximations via RDKit ETKDG \citep{rdkit}.
elements.id-string-435: \citet{torsional-diffusion} showed that RDKit is highly effective at generating conformations with correct bond distances and, as a result, can constrain the problem to a diffusion process over only torsion angles.
elements.id-string-436: We thus formalize MCG as modeling the conditional distribution $p(\mX | \gR)$, where $\gR$ is the RDKit generated atomic coordinates.
elements.id-string-437: This is functionally the same underlying distribution as $p(\mX | \emG)$, as we use RDKit as a building block to provide an approximation starting from only 2D information, $\gR = \text{RDKit ETKDG}(\emG)$.
elements.id-string-438: CREST~\citep{CREST} uses semi-empirical tight-binding density functional theory (DFT) for energy calculations, which, while computationally less expensive than ab-initio quantum mechanical (QM) methods, still requires approximately 90 core hours per drug-like molecule~\citep{GEOM}.
elements.id-string-439: Though CREST was used to generate the ``ground truth'' GEOM dataset, it is too slow for downstream applications such as high-throughput virtual screening.
elements.id-string-440: Cheminformatics methods, such as RDKit ETKDG, are commonly used to quickly generate approximate low-energy conformations of molecules.
elements.id-string-441: RDKit ETKDG employs a genetic algorithm for Distance Geometry optimization that can be enhanced with a molecular mechanics force field optimization (MMFF).
elements.id-string-442: DMCG \citep{DMCG} and Uni-Mol \citep{unimol} present examples of effective large models, the first mimicking the architecture of AlphaFold \citep{alphafold} and the second using large-scale SE(3)-equivariant transformer pre-training.
elements.id-string-443: \paragraph{Molecular Coarse-graining.} Molecular coarse-graining refers to the simplification of a molecule representation by grouping the fine-grained (FG) atoms in the original structure into individual coarse-grained (CG) beads with a rule-based mapping.\footnote{We use the terms CG graph nodes and beads interchangeably.}
elements.id-string-444: Coarse-graining has been widely utilized in protein design \citep{CGProt-background} and molecular dynamics~\citep{cg-force-field}, and analogously fragment-level or subgraph-level generation has proven to be highly valuable in diverse 2D molecule design tasks \citep{FaST}.
elements.id-string-445: Breaking down generative problems into smaller pieces can be applied to several 3D molecule tasks.
elements.id-string-446: We note that various coarse-graining strategies exist~\citep{cg-survey, arts2023diffusion, CG-MD, cg_thermo}, and many require the ability to represent inputs with a non-fixed granularity.
elements.id-string-447: We include an extensive discussion on further relevant work in Appendix \sref{section:related-work}.
elements.id-string-448: We discuss prominent 2D and 3D equivariant autoregressive molecular generation, protein docking, and structure-based drug discovery (SBDD) techniques, as well as our formal definition of SE(3)-equivariance.

elements.id-string-453: \paragraph{Learning Framework.} \model is a conditional generative model that learns $p(X | \gR)$ where $X$ is the low-energy 3D conformation, and $\gR$ is the RDKit approximate conformation.
elements.id-string-454: Specifically, we optimize $p(X | \gR)$ by maximizing its variational lower bound with an approximate conditional posterior distribution $q_\phi(z |X, \gR)$ and learned conditional prior $p_\psi(z | \gR)$:
elements.id-string-455: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \log p(X|\gR) \geq & \underbrace{\E_{q_\phi(z | X, \gR)} \log p_\theta(X | \gR, z)}_{\gL_{\text{reconstruction}}} + \underbrace{\E_{q_\phi(z | X, \gR)} \log \frac{ p_\psi(z|\gR) }{q_\phi(z| X, \gR)}}_{\gL_{\text{latent regularization}}}  + \gL_{\text{auxiliary}},  \end{aligned} \end{equation}
